It appears that prompting primary care providers about increased patient risk as a result of family history may not be effective in improving their ability to identify patients at high risk for certain conditions. While simple and at-the-visit family history prompts were found to be helpful in some cases, further studies are needed to examine physicians' perception of the utility of these prompts.

However, it seems that providers do benefit from more comprehensive outreach and service-based initiatives, such as those focused on clinical services, outreach, and breastfeeding. These types of programs may help increase access to care for low-income populations and improve overall health outcomes.

Additionally, having a usual physician can be an effective tool in improving access to care for low-income individuals, although its effectiveness is uncertain. Managed care programs have been shown to be helpful in linking more low-income persons to a medical home, but their impact on patient adherence to follow-up recommendations for abnormal Papanicolaou smears remains unclear.

Overall, it seems that a multifaceted approach involving multiple service-based initiatives and provider education may be needed to improve the identification of patients at high risk for certain conditions.
